docs.title: How Agents Made a Small Idea Worth Building
docs.text:
I wanted a catalogue of my open-source work for years. Agents changed the cost of getting from the idea to a working product, but experience still had to guide every important choice.

The result became Repo Showcase, a static catalogue and a reusable agent-guided workflow for publishing one person's repositories.

I wanted a page for the open-source applications I had written over the years. There were about fifty worth showing, spread across infrastructure, security, software delivery, and developer tooling.

The need was simple. The work behind it was not.

I would need to choose a static-site generator, decide where to host the page, work out how to collect repository data, define which projects belonged, create a useful set of filters, handle credentials, automate deployment, and decide how to keep the catalogue current. Each choice led to several more.

The site would be useful, but not useful enough to justify weeks of spare-time research and implementation. I had postponed it for years for a sensible reason: the likely reward was smaller than the cost of producing and maintaining it.

Agents changed that calculation.

I could delegate much of the research, comparison, code generation, and verification. My platform engineering experience still mattered because someone had to judge the options, find weak assumptions, and guide the work toward a maintainable result. The agent reduced the cost of applying that experience across hundreds of small decisions.

Agents made the idea practical because they reduced the cost of exploring choices and carrying out a plan. They did not remove the need for engineering judgement. They gave me enough reach to apply it throughout the project.

By Rodrigo A. Diaz Leven · LinkedIn · GitHub · Resume

docs.title: A small idea with a large decision surface
docs.text:
“Put my projects on a page” sounds like a weekend task. It can be, if the page is disposable.

I wanted something I could keep. That added questions before I wrote any code.

Was this a portfolio with ten featured projects or a catalogue of everything substantial? Should the page call GitHub whenever someone opened it, or should a build create static data? How would I distinguish projects I created from forks I kept for reference? Would repository language make a useful filter? How would I classify a Terraform module, a deployment tool, and an engineering essay without creating dozens of categories?

The operational questions were just as numerous. I needed to choose between Astro, Hugo, Eleventy, a React application, or plain HTML. I had to compare GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages, and paid hosting. A private source repository complicated some hosting options. A custom domain brought DNS and certificate work. Automated deployment required a credential, and that credential needed the smallest practical permissions.

Maintenance added another set. The page had to survive a GitHub API failure. It needed a refresh process for new repositories. A future change in branding should not require edits across many source files. If I released the project as a template, a new user should not publish my catalogue under their name by accident.

None of these decisions was especially hard on its own. Their combined cost had kept the idea in my backlog.

This is a common reason small tools remain unbuilt. The code is manageable, but the research, integration, and maintenance decisions make the effort hard to justify. A programmer can build the visible feature in a few evenings and still spend much longer working out the surrounding system.

docs.title: Research changed the economics of the project
docs.text:
I began with a research task rather than a coding prompt.

The agent received the outcome and the constraints: publish a catalogue of the public repositories I owned, exclude forks and weak entries, keep the source private, avoid a runtime service, and minimise ongoing cost. It inspected the account, read current documentation, compared tools, and recorded the evidence in a research note.

That first pass established the size and shape of the problem. My account had 66 public, non-fork repositories. Three were empty. Ten had no stars, views, or substantial content. Fifty-three belonged in the first catalogue.

The count mattered. Ten featured projects might fit a hand-written portfolio. Fifty-three needed filters, consistent metadata, and an automated refresh. It also showed why language alone would be a poor organising principle. Python, Go, Shell, Terraform, and PHP described implementation, while a visitor would care more about purpose and target platform.

The agent compared generators against the actual page rather than producing a generic list of popular frameworks. The site needed static HTML and a small amount of browser-side filtering. It did not need a server or a full client-rendered application. Astro, Hugo, and Eleventy all remained credible. Astro offered a direct fit because it rendered static HTML by default and let the filter carry the only client-side JavaScript.

Hosting research narrowed the next choice. The original instance lived in a private repository and produced a public site. GitHub Pages on my free plan could not publish directly from that private source. Cloudflare Pages could accept a built folder through Direct Upload without receiving repository access. Its free tier covered the expected use, so paying for a server would have added cost and operations without improving the result.

The research also addressed data freshness. Fetching GitHub at request time would keep the page current, but it would introduce a runtime, API limits, and another failure path. A committed JSON snapshot gave me static builds, reviewable changes, and a page that kept working when GitHub was unavailable. Refreshing the snapshot became an explicit maintenance action.

By the end of the research stage, I had a reasoned set of choices:

Concern Choice Reason Site generator Astro Static output with JavaScript limited to the filter Hosting Cloudflare Pages Free public hosting from a private source through Direct Upload Repository data Committed JSON snapshot Reviewable diffs and no runtime dependency on GitHub Catalogue scope Public, owned, non-fork repositories that pass explicit rules The page represents work I created and still want to present Organisation Purpose, platform, and language Readers can find relevant work without relying on one technical dimension

The agent did most of the collection and comparison. I reviewed whether the facts supported the recommendations. That division saved time without turning the decision into a popularity contest between tools.

docs.title: The stack followed the constraints
docs.text:
It would have been easy to choose Astro because it was current, or Cloudflare because I already used it. Research made the choices easier to defend and easier to change.

Hugo would have produced an excellent static site. Its speed offered little practical advantage for one page and fifty-three records. Astro fit my existing TypeScript tooling and made the interactive filter straightforward. That was enough. I did not need to prove that every other generator was bad.

The hosting choice followed the same pattern. I did not need a virtual machine for three static files. A paid host would not make the catalogue more accurate. Cloudflare Direct Upload let my own workflow build the site and send only the result. The host did not need read access to the private source repository.

Some choices emerged only after comparing approaches. Cloudflare's Git integration looked convenient, but it required a browser OAuth grant and repository access. It also committed the project to that integration mode. Direct Upload kept the build under my control and left open a future move to another static host.

The deploy credential needed separate thought. A broad account token would work, but it would give a simple site more authority than it deserved. The setup script therefore creates or accepts a Pages-only token. DNS changes use narrower, short-lived credentials. The standing deployment token cannot edit DNS.

These are platform engineering decisions applied to a personal site. They are also the reason I could guide the agent efficiently. I knew what kinds of coupling, permissions, and failure modes to question. The agent could inspect documentation and implement the answer once I chose the boundary.

Experience supplied the questions. The agent made it affordable to pursue each answer and preserve it in code, configuration, or documentation.

docs.title: Research needs an engineer in the loop
docs.text:
Agent research is fast, but speed does not guarantee a sound conclusion.

A later investigation into GitHub Pages corrected part of the first hosting analysis. A private repository could not publish a Pages site on my plan, but a separate public repository could hold only the built artifact. That two-repository arrangement kept the source private while giving GitHub Pages a public branch to serve.

The first conclusion had treated the source repository and publishing repository as the same object. The correction did not invalidate Cloudflare Pages for the main site. Cloudflare still handled several custom domains better, and the existing deployment worked. The new evidence added GitHub Pages as a useful second target and removed an unnecessary limitation from the reusable product.

This is how I want agent research to work. The output is a decision record, not scripture. Another agent or a later session can test an assumption, cite better evidence, and change the plan. Because the reasoning lives in files, the correction updates the project's memory rather than remaining in one chat transcript.

My role was to notice where an assumption constrained the design and ask for a focused investigation. The agent found the mechanisms, checked the live account, and documented which parts of the earlier argument still held.

docs.title: Planning turned the answer into an executable sequence
docs.text:
Research answered what to build and why. I still needed a safe order for the work.

A vague instruction such as “turn this site into an agentic template” would have produced a large change with many hidden dependencies. I asked the agent to create a plan with ordered work packages, explicit prerequisites, and acceptance commands.

The plan separated the project into stages:

Stage Work Establish the contract Put identity, catalogue policy, taxonomy, and sorting in validated configuration Remove instance assumptions Replace hardcoded account data and fix the empty first-run experience Give scripts an agent-friendly interface Add dry-run and machine-readable output, with consistent errors Encode the workflow Write focused skills for identity, curation, tagging, sorting, audit, deployment, and launch Prove behaviour Compare the new implementation with the live site Extract the product Separate the reusable public template from my configured instance Test a stranger's path Publish a small catalogue from prose without editing application code

The implementation plan eventually contained thirteen work packages. The first established the config contract because identity, filters, and scripts all depended on it. The skills came later because they needed stable commands and file ownership. Parity testing came before extracting the template. A smoke test on a separate account came last because success on the author's machine proves very little about reuse.

Each package ended with a command or observable result. A build had to reject an unknown tag by name. A renamed instance had to contain no trace of the old identity. The public template had to contain no private catalogue data. The deployed smoke-test site had to return the expected number of cards.

This planning stage reduced review cost. Instead of asking an agent for one large implementation, I could review one boundary at a time. Failures changed the next step while the rest of the plan stayed readable.

docs.title: My agent environment carried the working method
docs.text:
The project moved through several agent sessions. A long initial prompt would not have preserved enough context.

I used the repository as the shared memory. AGENTS.md files recorded conventions and boundaries. Research notes kept source comparisons and rejected options. The plan preserved sequence and dependencies. Repository-local skills described repeatable procedures and the checks that completed them.

That environment meant a new agent did not have to rediscover the whole project from commit history. It could read why the site used a committed snapshot, why tags came from a closed vocabulary, and why deployment used Direct Upload. The instructions also stated where the agent had to stop for a person, such as creating a credential in a browser or approving a destructive DNS change.

The skills became part of the application. A user can ask the agent to point the site at another account, change the inclusion rule, sort by stars, audit weak READMEs, or publish the result. Each skill owns a small part of the state and names the script that checks it.

This is the same environment I use for other agent-assisted engineering work. The domain changes, but the structure holds:

  • durable project guidance in AGENTS.md;
  • focused skills for recurring procedures;
  • research notes for decisions that depend on external facts;
  • a plan for work with dependencies;
  • deterministic checks at the end of each bounded change.

The agent had more than a request. It had a working method.

docs.title: Implementation became a series of bounded conversations
docs.text:
Once the research and plan existed, implementation stopped feeling like one large act of generation.

I could ask for the config contract and review the schema before touching the UI. I could test the empty state with an empty repository list. I could inspect how the curation rules treated the 66 candidates. When the tag classifier produced false positives, I changed the design so the agent inspected each repository and selected from a closed vocabulary.

The agent still wrote a large amount of code. It created the Astro components, fetch and deployment scripts, validation logic, docs, and skills. The important difference was that each change had a local purpose and a test.

Several defects appeared during this process. An identity check searched for the original site name, which could never catch a failed rename for a different user. Cloudflare provisioning succeeded while an old forwarding rule sent the public URL elsewhere. An unauthenticated refresh ran out of GitHub requests and risked producing a catalogue where healthy repositories looked empty.

Each failure improved the workflow. The identity skill now searches for the name being replaced. Deployment fetches the public URL before reporting success. Refresh aborts on incomplete data instead of writing a plausible but damaged snapshot.

Those corrections are a large part of the product. Code generation produced the first version quickly. The planned checks exposed where the first version was wrong.

docs.title: A real instance kept the abstraction honest
docs.text:
I built Repo Showcase from CodersCorp, the working catalogue for my own repositories. I kept the old site running while I built a second implementation next to it.

That gave the agent a concrete target. The new version had to show the same 53 repositories, tags, filter buttons, card fields, and sort order. A comparison script checked both deployments.

Only after parity passed did I extract the reusable public repository. The release process removed my identity, domains, and catalogue, then added a small sample so a fresh clone rendered a useful page. A release check compared the product with the instance and refused private data.

The final smoke test used another account and a one-repository allowlist. The agent configured and published the site from prose without changing files under src/. That proved the interface I cared about: a user could describe the catalogue they wanted, and the skills plus scripts could produce it.

Building against a real instance also prevented speculative features. I had actual repositories, real API limits, existing DNS, and an old site to compare. The agent could investigate concrete failures instead of designing for imagined ones.

docs.title: What agents changed for this class of idea
docs.text:
Before I used agents this way, the project had an unattractive cost profile. Most of the effort sat outside the final page:

  • reading product and hosting documentation;
  • comparing several valid stacks;
  • checking account limits and API behaviour;
  • turning preferences into configuration;
  • writing deployment automation and verification;
  • documenting enough of the system to maintain it later.

I could do all of that, but the result did not warrant the time.

Agents reduced the marginal cost of each step. A focused research request could compare hosting mechanisms and return evidence. A planning request could turn decisions into work packages. An implementation session could complete one package and run its acceptance checks. Another agent could review a specific assumption without reopening the whole design.

My experience increased the value of that speed. I could reject a full React runtime for a mostly static page, question a broad token, prefer a committed snapshot over a runtime dependency, and insist on a live URL check after deployment. Someone still had to know which trade-offs mattered.

The project became viable when generation and judgement worked together. The agent covered more ground than I would have justified covering alone. I kept the work aimed at a result I could operate and reuse.

docs.title: The practical method I would use again
docs.text: For another postponed idea, I would follow the same sequence.

docs.title: State the need and the constraints
docs.text: Describe the result in ordinary language. Include cost, privacy, maintenance, and operational limits. Avoid choosing the stack in the first sentence unless a real constraint has already chosen it.

docs.title: Ask for research that ends in a recommendation
docs.text: Require current evidence, viable alternatives, rejected options, and open decisions. Store the result in the repository so later work can test its assumptions.

docs.title: Review the decision, not every search step
docs.text: Use experience to challenge coupling, permissions, failure handling, and maintenance. Ask a narrower follow-up when a conclusion rests on an assumption.

docs.title: Convert the decision into ordered work
docs.text: Give each work package an observable acceptance check. Record dependencies. Put contracts and validation before orchestration.

docs.title: Teach the agent environment
docs.text: Keep stable guidance in AGENTS.md. Add a skill when a procedure will recur. Let skills call scripts rather than restating implementation logic in prose.

docs.title: Implement in bounded slices
docs.text: Review small changes against the plan. When a check exposes a bad assumption, update the workflow as well as the code.

docs.title: Prove the user's path
docs.text:
Test the result from a clean or separate instance. If the product promises configuration through conversation, verify that the agent can produce the result without source edits.

This process still takes work. It directs the expensive human attention toward choices and evidence, while agents handle much of the collection and execution.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Repo Showcase suited this approach because the risk was controlled. It publishes public repository metadata and static files. A mistake could break a site or misclassify a project, but it could not move money or expose customer records.

Higher-risk systems need stronger review, tests, and authority boundaries. An agent should not choose a destructive migration because its research summary sounds convincing. The same method can help, but the acceptance evidence and human approvals must match the consequences.

Agents also create review volume. A detailed plan can still produce too much code at once if the implementation ignores its package boundaries. I had to keep sessions focused and read the outputs that carried policy, especially config validation, credential scope, and deployment behaviour.

Research can be wrong or incomplete. The correction to the GitHub Pages analysis is evidence of that. Saving the reasoning made the mistake repairable; it did not make the first answer automatically correct.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
I had postponed a useful idea because its surrounding decisions cost more than the page seemed worth. Agents lowered that cost enough for me to proceed.

Research narrowed the options before code made any of them expensive. Planning turned the recommendation into a sequence I could review. Repository guidance and skills kept the method available across sessions. Deterministic scripts handled the repeated work and supplied evidence at each boundary.

My platform experience remained central. It helped me ask about static output, private source, token scope, runtime dependencies, DNS safety, and maintenance. The agent let me apply those questions across the whole project without spending weeks on every detail myself.

Turning an idea into reality with agents means using them to extend judgement, not bypass it. Research the choices, decide with evidence, plan the sequence, and make every implementation step prove what it changed.

Repo Showcase exists because that process made a modest idea economically sensible. I expect many useful internal tools, personal projects, and small products are waiting behind the same calculation.

docs.title: Deploying to Cloudflare Pages
docs.text:
The site is published by Direct Upload from a scoped API token, not by a Git-integrated Pages project. One command provisions everything, one command publishes.

npm run cf:setup     # once: mint the scoped token, create the Pages project
npm run deploy       # build and upload

docs.title: Why Direct Upload, not the Git integration
docs.text:
A Git-integrated Pages project builds on Cloudflare's side from a connected repository. It is the obvious choice, and it is the wrong one here, for three reasons:

  1. It is a one-way door. A project created with Git integration cannot later be switched to Direct Upload. Direct Upload can migrate the other way if it ever becomes necessary, so starting there keeps the option open.
  2. Connecting a repository needs a browser OAuth flow. The Cloudflare GitHub App is authorised by a human in a browser. No API token can install it, so the step cannot be automated and cannot be scripted for a fork.
  3. The repository is private. A Git integration has to be granted read access to it. Direct Upload needs no repository access at all — CI builds and uploads; Cloudflare never sees the source.

The cost of Direct Upload is that the build runs in CI rather than on Cloudflare. This build takes under a second and hits no network, because the catalogue is a committed snapshot.

docs.title: What npm run cf:setup creates
docs.text:
Object Detail API token <projectName>-pages-deploy, account-owned, Pages Write only Pages project <projectName>, production branch from the config .env keys CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN, CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID, mode 0600

It is idempotent. A second run reuses the working token and reports the existing project. --force rotates the token; --dry-run writes nothing.

docs.title: The admin token is used once
docs.text:
cf:setup needs a token with Account API Tokens: Write so it can mint the deploy token. That token is read from .env as cloudflare_admin_api_token, and it is never used for anything else.

The deploy token it produces carries Pages Write on one account and nothing else. A leaked deploy credential cannot touch DNS, Workers, R2, Access or billing. Delete cloudflare_admin_api_token from .env once CI has the deploy token — publishing does not need it again.

The admin token is not asked to touch Pages. It deliberately does not have that permission, so every Pages call is made with the narrow token. That is also the only way to prove the credential a publish will use is the one that works.

docs.title: The deploy token never holds DNS permission
docs.text:
The standing token carries Pages Write and nothing else, whether or not custom domains are configured.

Zone and DNS work needs permissions that must be scoped to exact zone ids, and those ids are discoverable only by a token that already holds Zone Read. A nested wildcard resource (…account.<id>.zone.*) is rejected at creation, so the ids have to be looked up first. cf:setup does that with two short-lived tokens:

Step Temporary token Lifetime Resolve hostname → zone Zone Read on the account 10 min Reconcile DNS records DNS Read + DNS Write on the resolved zones 20 min

Both are deleted in a finally, whether the work succeeded or threw. So the credential CI holds cannot edit DNS, even for a site with custom domains. That property is worth the extra round trip: a leaked deploy token can publish a bad page, not redirect your mail or take a hostname.

A Zone Read grant must be on the account resource. Granting it on a zone returns an empty zone list rather than an error, which reads as "this account has no domains".

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Everything site-specific lives in site.config.json. A fork edits this file and nothing else.

Key Meaning Default projectName Pages project name, and the *.pages.dev subdomain required productionBranch Branch name that owns the production alias main buildOutputDir Directory the build writes dist githubOwner Account whose repositories form the catalogue octocat customDomains Hostnames to serve, in addition to *.pages.dev [] tokenExpiryDays Deploy token lifetime; 0 means no expiry 365 deployTokenName Name of the token in the Cloudflare dashboard <projectName>-pages-deploy

projectName doubles as the subdomain, so Cloudflare accepts only lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. cf:setup rejects anything else before it creates anything.

customDomains is validated the same way: hostnames are lowercased and a trailing dot is stripped, but a duplicate is an error rather than being deduplicated, because a repeated hostname is a typo.

There is no wrangler.toml. cf-deploy.mjs passes the project name, branch and output directory to wrangler on the command line, so the config has one owner. A leftover wrangler.toml whose name disagrees is treated as an error, not a preference.

docs.title: Custom domains
docs.text:
List every hostname you want served. Apex and www are separate entries because they are separate DNS names:

"customDomains": ["coderscorp.com", "www.coderscorp.com"]

cf:setup does three things for each entry:

  1. Attaches it to the Pages project. Idempotent — an attached hostname is reported and skipped.
  2. Creates a proxied CNAME to <project>.pages.dev.
  3. Re-runs are free. A record already pointing at the right target is reported and left alone; a record pointing at the right target with the proxy off just gets the proxy enabled.

docs.title: Apex is not a special case
docs.text: A plain DNS CNAME is illegal at a zone apex, and an apex usually already holds SPF, DMARC and verification TXT records. Cloudflare's proxied CNAME is different: measured on a live zone, a proxied CNAME at the apex was accepted alongside two existing TXT records and served correctly. So the apex needs no special handling, and the mail records are untouched.

docs.title: Attaching a domain does not create its DNS record
docs.text: Measured: after POST …/pages/projects/<name>/domains returned 200, the zone still had no record for that hostname, and the domain sat in initializing until the record existed. The two steps are separate, which is why DNS permission is needed at all.

docs.title: Records that point somewhere else
docs.text:
If an A, AAAA or CNAME already exists at the hostname, it points at something else — possibly a live service. cf:setup refuses to replace it and exits non-zero:

! coderscorp.com points elsewhere (A 65.108.126.170)
  pass --overwrite-dns to point it at coderscorp.pages.dev

--overwrite-dns deletes those records and creates the CNAME. TXT, MX and every other type are never touched. This is a separate flag on purpose: a mistyped hostname should not silently take a domain off the internet.

docs.title: Certificates take a few minutes
docs.text:
A new hostname starts as pending or initializing while Cloudflare issues a certificate. Requests fail until it completes. Watch it with:

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN" \
  "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID/pages/projects/<name>/domains" \
  | jq '.result[] | {name, status, verification_data}'

docs.title: www and apex both serve; neither redirects
docs.text:
Both hostnames serve identical content. That is what "load from both" means, and it is what Cloudflare gives you when both are attached.

If you want a canonical hostname, that is a separate decision with a separate mechanism — a Cloudflare redirect rule or a _redirects file in the build output. Neither is configured here, because the choice (apex → www or the reverse) belongs to the operator.

docs.title: Something can answer before Pages
docs.text:
cf:setup fetches every hostname at the end and reports what it actually serves, because provisioning can succeed while the site is unreachable.

The measured case: a forwarding Page Rule on the zone sent every path to a fixed URL, so coderscorp.com/, /index.html and /anything/else all returned 302 to the same place and Pages never saw the request. No DNS record and no Pages setting can override that.

A Page Rule is invisible to an account-owned token. GET …/pagerules returns 1011 Page Rules endpoint does not support account owned tokens, and that is not a permissions problem — no account token can read them, at any permission level. Only a user-owned token, or the dashboard, can see or remove one.

So cf:setup detects the symptom and tells you where to look:

! example.com: redirects to https://github.com/octocat
  · a redirect rule or Page Rule on the zone is answering before Pages

The fix is manual: Cloudflare dashboard → the zone → Rules → Page Rules → delete or disable the forwarding rule. Then re-run npm run cf:setup to confirm.

A path-preserving redirect is a different shape and worth distinguishing: if /foo lands on …/foo, the rule is forwarding with a path variable. A fixed target for every path — what happened here — is a plain static forward.

docs.title: ENOTFOUND from the verification step is usually local
docs.text:
cf:setup runs on your machine and uses the OS resolver, which can hold a negative or stale answer for a hostname that was created minutes ago. The step reports the socket code for exactly this reason:

· example.com: could not connect (ENOTFOUND)
  local DNS may not have the new record yet; the site can still be live

Check with a public resolver before believing it:

dig +short @1.1.1.1 A example.com
curl -sI --resolve "example.com:443:$(dig +short @1.1.1.1 A example.com | head -1)" https://example.com/

docs.title: From this machine
docs.text:
npm run deploy                  # production branch
npm run deploy -- --branch x    # preview deployment
npm run deploy -- --skip-build  # upload dist/ as it stands
npm run deploy -- --dry-run     # build, then print the upload command

The token is read from .env and passed to wrangler through the environment, never on the command line — an argument is visible in ps.

docs.title: From GitHub Actions
docs.text:
.github/workflows/deploy.yml publishes on every push to main. It reads the project name, branch and output directory from site.config.json rather than duplicating them, so renaming the site needs no workflow edit.

Add two repository secrets once:

gh secret set CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN --body "$(grep '^CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=' .env | cut -d= -f2-)"
gh secret set CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID --body "2e9c09b27d2a089c531b12ae0f0e6ff3"

The workflow fails with an explicit message when CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN is missing, rather than deploying nothing and reporting success.

docs.title: Rotating and revoking
docs.text:
npm run cf:setup -- --force   # revoke the old token, mint a new one, update .env

A mint always revokes the previous token of the same name, so the account holds exactly one deploy credential per site. Without that rule a re-run leaves a second token with an identical name — a credential nobody can identify and nobody dares delete.

When rotating in CI, update the repository secret after the local rotation. Both the old and new token work until the old one is revoked, so the order does not matter.

To revoke everything: delete the token at https://dash.cloudflare.com/profile/api-tokens. The Pages project and its deployments are unaffected; only future publishes fail.

docs.title: What was measured, and what it cost to learn
docs.text:
These are observations from this account on 2026-10-30, not documentation claims. Each one broke something first.

Finding Detail Account-owned tokens verify elsewhere /user/tokens/verify returns 1000 Invalid API Token for a valid account-owned token. /accounts/{id}/tokens/verify is the correct endpoint, and trying both is the only reliable check. Account API Tokens: Write grants no Pages access The token that can mint tokens cannot list Pages projects. Provisioning must mint first, then act. The Pages projects endpoint rejects per_page ?per_page=25 and ?per_page=100 both return 8000024 Invalid list options provided. ?page=N works. This looks like ordinary pagination and silently breaks the call. expires_on rejects milliseconds It wants 2005-12-30T01:02:03Z. JavaScript's toISOString() emits .234Z, which is rejected with the whole payload echoed back. A 400 and an auth failure look the same behind a retry loop The first version retried on any error and reported "cannot reach the Pages API", which hid a query-parameter bug behind a permissions story. The retry now returns the last error. Attaching a Pages domain creates no DNS record POST …/pages/projects/<name>/domains returned 200 with status initializing, and the zone still had no record for the hostname. Zone Read does not read DNS records It lists zones. /zones/{id}/dns_records still returns 403. Records need DNS Read, a separate zone-scoped permission. Zone Read on a zone resource shows nothing It must be granted on the account resource. Zone-scoped, it returns an empty list instead of an error, which reads as "no domains in this account". Zone resources cannot be wildcarded com.cloudflare.api.account.<id>.zone.* is rejected with 1001 Token creation request was rejected, alone and combined with an account-scoped policy. Only exact zone ids are accepted, so the ids must be discovered before a DNS-scoped token can be minted. A proxied CNAME is legal at an apex with TXT records A plain CNAME cannot coexist with SPF or DMARC, but Cloudflare accepted a proxied CNAME at the apex alongside two TXT records and served it. Page Rules are closed to account-owned tokens GET …/pagerules returns 1011 Page Rules endpoint does not support account owned tokens with every account permission granted. No account-owned credential can read or edit a Page Rule. A forwarding Page Rule wins over Pages With a proxied CNAME to Pages in place, every path still returned 302 to the rule's fixed target. DNS and Pages settings cannot override it.

Resource keys for account-owned tokens need the account id: com.cloudflare.api.account.<account_id>. Bare com.cloudflare.api.account and the wildcard com.cloudflare.api.account.* are both rejected with 1001.

docs.title: Checking the deployment
docs.text:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://<projectName>.pages.dev

To confirm the catalogue actually rendered rather than merely returning 200:

curl -s https://<projectName>.pages.dev/ | grep -c 'class="card"'

The dashboard is at https://dash.cloudflare.com/<accountId>/pages/view/<projectName>, and npm run cf:setup prints the exact URL.

docs.title: Hosting
docs.text: Two hosts are supported and site.config.json decides which ones publish. The rule throughout is that judgement lives in the config and the scripts obey it: no script decides a host, and no host decides a domain.

docs.title: The four modes
docs.text:
Mode Config Served at Needs GitHub Pages, no domain targets: ["github-pages"], no customDomain <owner>.github.io/<repo>/ a GitHub account GitHub Pages, custom domain targets: ["github-pages"], customDomain set that domain, at its root a GitHub account and a domain Cloudflare Pages, no domain targets: ["cloudflare-pages"], no domains <projectName>.pages.dev a Cloudflare account Cloudflare Pages, custom domain targets: ["cloudflare-pages"], domains set those domains a Cloudflare account and a domain

The shipped config is the first row. It is the only mode that needs no second account, no domain and no token, so it is the one a new user meets first.

docs.title: Config shape
docs.text:
"deploy": {
  "targets": ["cloudflare-pages", "github-pages"],
  "cloudflarePages": {
    "customDomains": ["example.net", "www.example.net"]
  },
  "githubPages": {
    "repository": "example-gh",
    "branch": "gh-pages",
    "customDomain": "example.com"
  }
}

githubPages.repository is optional. Omitted, the artifact is published to the repository the source lives in, which needs no credential. Set to owner/name, it goes to a separate public repository — the shape a private source needs.

githubPages.customDomain is a single hostname, not a list, because GitHub stores exactly one in the CNAME file. Its www sibling is derived: GitHub redirects between them once the DNS records exist.

docs.title: One apex per site
docs.text:
GitHub Pages allows one apex domain per site, plus its www. Two apex domains need two sites. This is why a deployment with two domains usually keeps one on Cloudflare: it is not a preference, it is the only arrangement that serves both.

A project site with a custom domain is served at that domain's root, so its base path is / and the build is the same one Cloudflare receives. A project site without one is served under /<repo>/, so npm run build:gh sets base and every asset URL carries the prefix.

docs.title: What each host needs at DNS
docs.text:
GitHub Pages, apex and www, records not proxied:

example.com       A      185.199.108.153
                        185.199.109.153
                        185.199.110.153
                        185.199.111.153
www.example.com   CNAME  <owner>.github.io

www must point at <owner>.github.io and never at the apex: GitHub documents that pointing a subdomain at the apex breaks HTTPS enforcement.

Cloudflare Pages owns its records through its own proxy, and needs no manual records once npm run cf:setup has run.

docs.title: Three ways this breaks quietly
docs.text:
1. Missing .nojekyll. The build writes CSS and JS to _astro/, and Jekyll drops directories beginning with an underscore. The page returns 200 and renders unstyled. gh-deploy.mjs writes the file; a hand-rolled deploy must too.
  2. A lost CNAME. On a branch deploy the domain lives in the CNAME file. A force-push that does not include it removes the domain. gh-deploy.mjs regenerates it from the config on every run.
  3. A domain change with no deploy. Adding or removing a custom domain changes the routing path but does not rebuild the site, so asset links stay broken until something is pushed. That is what --force is for.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Nothing is required for the default mode. When a target does need a credential, it is written into .env by the user — never pasted into a conversation, an issue or a commit. npm run secrets:check answers "is it there" without printing the value.

Key Needed by CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN, CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID cloudflare-pages GH_TOKEN github-pages to an external repository, when SSH is unavailable GITHUB_TOKEN npm run refresh, optional, for view counts

GH_TOKEN is optional on purpose: a local deploy pushes over SSH with the key the operator already has. It is required only in CI, where no key exists.

docs.title: Repo Showcase
docs.text:
A catalogue page for everything you shipped, set up by asking an agent for it.

Live at: https://bruj0.net/

One deployment with 53 repositories. The sample this repository ships has six.

Every public repository you own is a finished argument that almost nobody can find. GitHub sorts your profile by last push, and each entry is a name, a language, and one line of description. Nothing there says what the project does, what it runs on, or whether it is finished.

Repo Showcase turns the same account into a page that answers those questions: one card per repository, filters for what it does and where it runs, and four ways to sort. It is static HTML rendered by Astro and published to GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages, so there is no server, no database, and no call to GitHub at runtime. The catalogue is a JSON file you commit, which means every change to the page arrives as a reviewable diff.

docs.title: The stack
docs.text:
Piece Choice What it buys Generator Astro 7, static output One HTML file, one stylesheet, one icon Host Cloudflare Pages, GitHub Pages, or both A key in the config decides; no code changes Data A JSON snapshot committed to the repo Builds need no network; every catalogue change is a reviewable diff Filtering Plain JavaScript in the page No framework runtime and no bundle to audit Server none Nothing to patch, restart or pay for Database none Nothing to back up, migrate or leak Config site.config.json One file decides brand, account, rules, host and domains Build Node 22 or later One command, no network Licence MIT Fork it and change the brand

Measured on a catalogue of 53 repositories: three files, 110 KB. The catalogue is inlined into the page for search, so filtering makes no network request.

What it does

  • Search, filters for purpose, platform and language, and four sort modes, all applied in the browser.
  • Renders the full catalogue into the HTML. JavaScript filters it; it does not build it, so the page still reads with scripts blocked.
  • Makes no third-party request: no web fonts, no analytics, no CDN script. The only external URLs are the ones the page links to.
  • Publishes to one host or both, chosen by deploy.targets.

What it deliberately does not do

  • No login, comments, telemetry or contact form. Each one adds a server or a third party, which is the cost this design exists to avoid.
  • No server rendering and no API routes. Static output only.

docs.title: Why you would use it
docs.text:
You have You get Forty repositories and no index of them One page, filterable by purpose, platform and language A CV that claims breadth A page that shows it, with links that resolve No appetite for another service to run Static files, no server and no database A catalogue that goes stale npm run refresh rewrites the data as a diff you can read

A domain is optional and so is Cloudflare. Without either, the site publishes to GitHub Pages. See Where it publishes.

docs.title: Why it is built around an agent
docs.text:
Most site generators ask you to learn their config format. This one asks you to describe what you want, in a sentence.

You say It writes "Drop anything with no stars and fewer than ten files." catalogue.unnoticed = { maxStars: 0, maxViews: 0, maxFiles: 10 } "Sort them by stars." sort.default = "stars" "Point this at my account." githubOwner, and the brand strings that use {githubOwner} "Only these repositories belong." catalogue.include = [...]

The division is deliberate: judgement belongs in prose, determinism belongs in scripts. The agent decides what you meant and writes one key. The scripts read that key and never guess. No line of code decides which repositories are yours, which is why the same tree publishes a catalogue of 53 for one account and a catalogue of one for another without a source change.

Seven skills in .agents/skills/ carry the procedure, and site-launch sequences the other six. It asks the five questions only you can answer — which account, what the site is called, which repositories belong, a domain or a *.pages.dev subdomain, and whether to mint a token or paste one — then hands control back wherever a credential or a browser is needed, and resumes where it stopped.

Each skill ends by checking its own work. site-identity greps the build for the name you are leaving behind. catalogue-curate reports the counts its rules produced. site-deploy fetches the URL and looks for the catalogue before it says "published". A skill that cannot check itself is a prompt, not a skill.

site.config.json        your site: name, brand, account, domains, sort order
catalogue/tags.json     purpose, platform and language for each repository
catalogue/excluded.json what the rules left out, and why
src/data/repos.json     the catalogue snapshot the page renders
.agents/skills/         seven skills that edit the four files above

docs.title: What you must supply
docs.text: You need Why Without it A GitHub account The catalogue is built from its public repositories, and GitHub Pages hosts the site Nothing to list, and nowhere to publish Node 22 or later The build and the scripts Nothing runs A Cloudflare account Optional. A second host, with a CDN and preview deployments You publish to GitHub Pages only A domain Optional. Your own address instead of *.github.io The site lives at <owner>.github.io/<repo>/

docs.title: Where it publishes
docs.text:
Two hosts are supported and the config decides which ones are used.

Mode Served at Needs GitHub Pages, no domain <owner>.github.io/<repo>/ a GitHub account, nothing else GitHub Pages, custom domain your domain, at its root a GitHub account and a domain Cloudflare Pages, no domain <projectName>.pages.dev a Cloudflare account Cloudflare Pages, custom domain your domain a Cloudflare account and a domain

The shipped site.config.json uses the first mode, so npm run deploy works with nothing configured. Enabling a second host is a change to deploy.targets, not a change to any script.

An agent will ask before enabling Cloudflare, and will never ask you to paste a secret into the conversation: the token goes in .env, and npm run secrets:check reports whether it is there without printing it.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
npm install

# 1. Say who the site is for
$EDITOR site.config.json      # githubOwner, brand.name, projectName

# 2. Pull the catalogue
#    Optional GITHUB_TOKEN raises the rate limit and enables view counts.
GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) npm run refresh

# 3. Look at it
npm run dev

# 4. Publish
npm run deploy                # to <owner>.github.io/<repo>/

Steps 1 to 4 need a GitHub account and nothing else. Cloudflare is an opt-in that adds a host; it never becomes a requirement for the first publish.

docs.title: The skill path
docs.text:
The four data files are meant to be edited by an agent, not by hand. The skills in .agents/skills/ read and write them, and each one states how to check its own work:

Skill Trigger it with site-launch "set this up", "publish my repositories" site-identity "rename the site", "point this at my account" catalogue-curate "which repos belong", "drop the empty ones" catalogue-tag "tag my repos", "categorise by purpose" catalogue-sort "sort by stars", "newest first" catalogue-audit "which repos need a README" site-deploy "deploy", "publish this", "set up the domain"

site-launch sequences the other six and stops wherever a person has to act: creating a token in the Cloudflare dashboard, deleting a forwarding rule, waiting for a certificate, creating a throwaway repository.

Both Claude Code and VS Code read .agents/skills/ as-is; no plugin is installed and no config is written.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Does npm run dev Local dev server npm run build Static build to dist/ npm run preview Serve the build npm run refresh Re-fetch the catalogue from GitHub into src/data/repos.json npm run check:config Prove the JavaScript and Python config loaders agree npm run cf:setup One-time: create the Pages project, mint or accept a deploy token npm run deploy Build and publish npm run compare:sites <a> <b> Report how two builds or two live sites differ

Every script in scripts/ also accepts --json and --dry-run, so an agent can ask what a command would do before it does it.

docs.title: The published documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is published at bruj0.github.io/reposhowcase, built with MkDocs Material and deployed to the gh-pages branch by .github/workflows/docs.yml.

The landing page is the long-form essay — the account of how this project was researched, planned and built. The rest of the site is this README, Deployment and Hosting:

Page Source / (essay) essay/index.md, generated from the author's personal-docs /readme/ README.md /deployment/ docs/deployment.md /hosting/ docs/hosting.md

npm run docs:assemble copies those four documents into site_src/, which is what MkDocs reads. The staging step exists because MkDocs copies everything under docs_dir into the site, so pointing it at the repository root would publish node_modules/ and dist/. Nothing is edited under site_src/.

The essay has a canonical copy outside this repository, so its page is generated rather than hand-edited:

node scripts/sync-essay.mjs           # regenerate essay/index.md
node scripts/sync-essay.mjs --check   # exit 1 when the copy has drifted
npm run docs:assemble                  # rebuild site_src/

ESSAY_SOURCE overrides the canonical path. To build the site locally:

uv venv .venv --python 3.12
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -r requirements-docs.txt
npm run docs:assemble
.venv/bin/mkdocs build --strict --site-dir _site   # or: .venv/bin/mkdocs serve

docs.title: The sample catalogue
docs.text:
src/data/repos.json ships with six public repositories — Ansible, Kubernetes, Hugo, Oh My Zsh, mdBook and Composer. They are not the author's and they are not endorsed by this project: they are there so the page renders with real content on the first build. npm run refresh replaces the file with your own repositories.

Until you run it, the site says so, in the lede and in the eyebrow.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Nothing secret is committed. .env is gitignored; .env.example lists every key and says which step writes it.

Key Written by Used by cloudflare_admin_api_token you, by hand, once cf:setup only, and only when minting CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN cf:setup deploy CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID cf:setup both GITHUB_TOKEN you, by hand refresh

Two ways to get a deploy token, and the README cannot pick for you:

  • Mint one. Needs an admin token with Account API Tokens: Write. Narrower at the end, but you have to create a privileged credential first.
  • Paste one. Create a token with Cloudflare Pages: Edit in the dashboard and paste it. cf:setup --no-mint accepts it and skips the admin token entirely.

A pasted token cannot edit DNS. If you asked for a custom domain, cf:setup prints the CNAME each hostname needs and leaves it to you, rather than pretending to have made it.

docs.title: Requirements that are not obvious
docs.text:
• Cloudflare Pages is deployed by Direct Upload, not by Git integration. The Git integration needs a browser OAuth grant and repository read access, and it is a one-way door once chosen.
  • A custom domain needs DNS permission on the exact zone. Zone Read lists zones; it does not read or write records. The deploy token is scoped to the zone ids the setup step discovered.
  • Page Rules are closed to account-owned API tokens. If a rule redirects your hostname, no API call in this repository can remove it. cf:setup detects the redirect and stops.
  • projectName is both the Pages project and its *.pages.dev subdomain. Change it before the first deploy. Renaming later leaves the old project and its hostname behind in the account, because nothing deletes what it did not create.
